reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India national programmes
clinicalPearls: The most common soil-transmitted helminth worldwide, acquired by ingesting embryonated eggs from faecally contaminated food, water or soil
Most infections are light and asymptomatic; heavy worm loads, especially in children, cause malnutrition and growth impairment
During larval lung migration patients may develop a transient eosinophilic pneumonitis (Loeffler syndrome) with cough, wheeze and pulmonary infiltrates
Heavy intestinal burdens can cause bowel obstruction, particularly in children, and adult worms can migrate into the biliary or pancreatic ducts causing obstruction, cholangitis or pancreatitis
It is highly prevalent in parts of India with inadequate sanitation and is targeted by school-based mass deworming programmes
Diagnosis is usually by detecting characteristic eggs on stool microscopy; adult worms may be seen passed in stool or vomit or on imaging
Antiparasitic (anthelmintic) therapy is highly effective for uncomplicated intestinal infection
Biliary or obstructive complications may require endoscopic or surgical intervention in addition to anthelmintics
reference.pathophysiology: Ingested Ascaris eggs hatch in the small intestine; larvae penetrate the gut wall, travel via the portal circulation to the liver and then the lungs, break into the alveoli, ascend the tracheobronchial tree, are swallowed, and mature into large adult worms in the small intestine. The pulmonary phase provokes an eosinophilic hypersensitivity reaction. In the gut, large numbers of worms can form a bolus that obstructs the lumen, and individual worms may migrate into the biliary tree, pancreatic duct or appendix, producing obstructive and inflammatory complications. Chronic infection contributes to malabsorption and nutritional deficits.
additionalDifferentials: Other intestinal helminth infections (hookworm, Trichuris, Strongyloides)
Mechanical bowel obstruction of other cause
Gallstone disease or other biliary obstruction
infectionMimics: Asthma or allergic bronchopulmonary disease during the pulmonary phase
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count for eosinophilia, especially during larval migration
Abdominal ultrasound or imaging to detect worms in bowel or biliary tree
Chest imaging if eosinophilic pneumonitis is suspected
Endoscopic evaluation for hepatobiliary or pancreatic complications
redFlags: Features of intestinal obstruction (distension, vomiting, absent stool/flatus), particularly in a child
Biliary obstruction, cholangitis or pancreatitis from worm migration
Respiratory distress during the pulmonary migratory phase
Signs of peritonitis suggesting bowel perforation from a heavy worm bolus
reference.prognosis: Uncomplicated infection has an excellent prognosis and responds promptly to anthelmintic treatment. Morbidity arises from heavy infections causing nutritional compromise in children and from obstructive complications, which can occasionally be life-threatening if not treated in time.
pitfalls: Overlooking ascariasis as a cause of paediatric bowel obstruction in endemic areas
Missing biliary or pancreatic migration as the cause of acute abdominal pain
Attributing migratory pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia to asthma alone
Neglecting sanitation and re-treatment, allowing reinfection
management: Anthelmintic eradication with a benzimidazole such as albendazole or mebendazole, with pyrantel pamoate as an alternative, to clear adult intestinal worms
Nutritional rehabilitation and micronutrient repletion in children with heavy burdens and growth impairment
Supportive care for the pulmonary migratory phase (Loeffler syndrome), with bronchodilators and corticosteroids reserved for significant hypersensitivity symptoms
Management of intestinal obstruction initially with fluids, nasogastric decompression and anthelmintics, reserving surgery for failure, perforation or volvulus
Endoscopic or surgical intervention for hepatobiliary or pancreatic-duct migration causing cholangitis or pancreatitis, with appropriate antimicrobial cover
Sanitation and hygiene measures plus participation in school- or community-based mass deworming programmes, with treatment of affected household contacts
Follow-up stool microscopy after treatment to confirm clearance and detect reinfection
